title: Hip and knee osteoarthritis: safer ways to get up from a chair, bed, toilet and car (UK guide)
meta_title: Hip and Knee Arthritis: Getting Up Safely (UK)
meta_description: Hip and knee osteoarthritis: safer ways to stand from a chair, get in and out of bed, use the toilet and get into a car, plus aids that help (UK).
excerpt: Hip and knee osteoarthritis: safer ways to stand from a chair, get in and out of bed, use the toilet and get into a car, plus aids that help (UK).
direct_answer: Getting up from a chair, bed, toilet or car seat is one of the hardest jobs with hip or knee osteoarthritis. The same steps help almost every time: shuffle to the front of the seat, put your feet back slightly, lean forward so your nose is over your toes, then push up with your hands and pause before you walk. Higher, firmer seats make it easier, and equipment such as a raised toilet seat or furniture raisers can help. Practising sit-to-stand every day strengthens the muscles you need. If you have had a hip replacement, follow your surgical team's advice. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself.

content:
With hip or knee osteoarthritis, the moments of moving from sitting to standing, or the other way, often hurt most and are when people are most likely to wobble or fall. A few simple steps, the right seat height and a little daily practice make a real difference.

This guide covers the basics for every transfer. For more detail on each one, see getting up from a chair, getting in and out of bed, getting into a car and toilet frames. It is also for carers who help someone up.

The basic way to stand up

  1. Shuffle to the front edge of the seat.
  2. Put your feet slightly back, hip-width apart. If one leg is more painful, put the better foot a little further back.
  3. Put your hands on the armrests or the seat beside you.
  4. Lean forward until your nose is over your toes.
  5. Push up through your hands and legs together.
  6. Stand still for a moment before you walk, and pick up your stick or frame once you are steady.

Do not pull yourself up on a walking frame: it can tip.

The basic way to sit down

  1. Walk right up to the seat and turn until you feel it against the back of your legs.
  2. Reach back for the armrests one hand at a time.
  3. Lean forward slightly and lower yourself slowly. Do not drop.

Chair height and type

Low, soft sofas are the hardest to get out of. A firm chair with arms, at a height where your hips are level with or slightly above your knees, is usually easiest. Furniture raisers or a riser chair can help. See rise and recline chairs before buying one.

Bed

To get out: roll onto your side, bring your knees to the edge, push up with your arms as your legs go down, then sit on the edge for a moment before standing. A firm mattress, a bed at the right height and a bed lever can help.

Toilet

Toilets are often low. A raised toilet seat, a toilet frame or a grab rail lets you push up with your hands. Ask an occupational therapist what suits your bathroom.

Car

Push the seat back and recline it a little. Stand with your back to the seat, sit down first, then swing your legs in together. A plastic bag on the seat can help you turn. Reverse the steps to get out.

Bath

Getting down into and up from a bath is hard with hip or knee arthritis. A bath board, bath lift or a shower may be safer. An occupational therapist can advise. See what to do while you wait for an OT.

Practise to get stronger

Sit-to-stand is also an exercise. Practise standing up and sitting down slowly a few times, once or twice a day, using your hands as much as you need. As it gets easier, use your hands less. NICE recommends exercise as a core treatment for osteoarthritis, and a physiotherapist can tailor it to you. Take your usual pain relief as advised by your GP or pharmacist so you can move.

After a hip or knee replacement

Follow the advice your hospital team gave you. They may ask you to avoid low seats or certain positions for a while.

When to see your GP

See your GP or a physiotherapist if getting up is getting harder, you are having falls or near-falls, or pain stops you sleeping. Your GP can review pain relief, refer you to physiotherapy or a falls service, and talk about whether you need to see a surgeon.

Ask NHS 111 or your GP for same-day advice if a hip or knee becomes hot, red and swollen, or you feel unwell with a fever. Call 999 if you cannot put weight on a leg after a fall, the leg looks shortened or turned out, or someone has fallen and cannot get up.

For carers and family

Let the person do as much as they can and guide with your words. Do not pull on arms or let them hold your neck. If you are lifting someone, ask for an occupational therapist assessment. If a fall happens, follow the falls plan and only help someone up if they are not hurt.

Common questions

Why is getting up the most painful part?

Stiff joints and weak thigh muscles mean the hip and knee have to work hardest as you rise. Moving your weight forward first takes some of the load off.

Is it bad to use my arms?

No. Using armrests is safer. Practise using them a little less over time to build strength.
